posts.body: The Weil conjectures project relies heavily on category theory, particularly derived categories. This has presented challenges at two different levels: technical difficulties, most notably with the performance of Lean’s kernel, and broader questions about how to choose and organize the mathematical constructions underlying the formalization. Here we describe several concrete problems we encountered, how we addressed them, and what they taught us about formalization on this scale. ## 1 Kernel Checking and Performance Our extensive use of category theory has exposed several serious performance bottlenecks, the most severe of which arose during kernel checking rather than tactic elaboration. In such cases, Lean could elaborate a proof term relatively quickly, yet the kernel would take an unexpectedly long time to check it or establish a required definitional equality. Although we do not have a complete explanation for every slowdown, the following cases illustrate ways to avoid some of the most costly comparisons. ### 1.1 Timeout in the Base-Change Morphism Our first major example arose while proving an `_app` lemma for the base-change morphism, viewed as a natural transformation. For a commutative square, we construct this morphism in three steps using the adjunction $f^* \dashv f_*$: $$ \begin{CD} X' @>{g'}>> X \\ @V{f'}VV @VV{f}V \\ Y' @>>{g}> Y \end{CD} $$ $$ \mathrm{Ex} : g^*Rf_* \to Rf'_*f'^*(g^*Rf_*) \to Rf'_*g'^*(f^*Rf_*) \to Rf'_*g'^*. $$ The most complicated part was the middle step, which transports the composition of functors across the commutative square and set up `_app` lemma. ```lean def Etale.baseChangeSquareStep (sq : CommSq g' f' f g) : (R(f)_*[A]+ ⋙ (g)^*[A].mapDerivedCategoryPlus) ⋙ ((f')^*[A].mapDerivedCategoryPlus ⋙ R(f')_*[A]+) ≅ (R(f)_*[A]+ ⋙ (f)^*[A].mapDerivedCategoryPlus) ⋙ ((g')^*[A].mapDerivedCategoryPlus ⋙ R(f')_*[A]+) := Functor.associator _ _ _ ≪≫ Functor.isoWhiskerLeft R(f)_*[A]+ ((Functor.associator _ _ _).symm ≪≫ Functor.isoWhiskerRight (pullbackSquareComparison A sq) R(f')_*[A]+ ≪≫ Functor.associator _ _ _) ≪≫ (Functor.associator _ _ _).symm ``` *Code excerpt 1: The original square-transport construction.* ```lean lemma Etale.baseChangeSquareStep_app (sq : CommSq g' f' f g) (K : DerivedCategory.Plus (Sheaf X.smallEtaleTopology A)) : ((Etale.baseChangeSquareStep A sq).app K) = R(f')_*[A]+.mapIso ((pullbackSquareComparison A sq).app (R(f)_*[A]+.obj K)) ``` We expected `simp` to complete this proof. Elaboration was relatively quick, but the kernel timed out. Even after simplifying the expression, proofs using either `simp` or `rfl` still timed out. This was our first indication that the bottleneck lay in kernel checking, not in finding a proof through elaboration. Our initial workaround was to replace the specific pullback and pushforward functors with abstract functors. We proved a general square-transport construction and its `_app` lemmas at that level, then specialized those results to base change: ```lean def squareTransport {G₁ : C₂ ⥤ C₃} {G₂ : C₃ ⥤ C₄} {G₃ : C₂ ⥤ C₃'} {G₄ : C₃' ⥤ C₄} (R : C₁ ⥤ C₂) (R' : C₄ ⥤ C₅) (θ : G₁ ⋙ G₂ ≅ G₃ ⋙ G₄) : (R ⋙ G₁) ⋙ (G₂ ⋙ R') ≅ (R ⋙ G₃) ⋙ (G₄ ⋙ R') ``` *Code excerpt 2: An abstract square-transport construction.* This resolved the immediate problem, but we encountered a similar issue later when proving an `_app` lemma for base change of the exceptional pushforward $f_!$. In that construction, the base-change morphism appeared as one component of a longer composite: ```lean def Etale.lowerShriekBaseChange (c : Compactification f) (sq : IsPullback g' f' f g) : Rf_!(c)[A]+ ⋙ D+((g)^*[A]) ⟶ D+((g')^*[A]) ⋙ Rf_!(c.baseChange sq)[A]+ := (Functor.associator _ _ _).hom ≫ Functor.whiskerLeft D+((c.i)_!open[A]) (Etale.baseChange A (c.baseChange_isPullback_g sq).toCommSq) ≫ (Functor.associator _ _ _).inv ≫ Functor.whiskerRight (Etale.openImmersionLowerShriekBaseChangeIso A (c.baseChange_isPullback_i sq)).hom R+(((c.baseChange sq).g)_*[A]) ≫ (Functor.associator _ _ _).hom ``` *Code excerpt 3: Base change for the exceptional pushforward.* This made us reconsider the case-specific workaround: while it avoided an individual timeout, it did not address the underlying difficulty in a principled or sustainable way. We therefore marked `Etale.baseChange` with `@[no_expose]`. In this case, preventing downstream code from unfolding that definition was enough to avoid the expensive kernel reduction. This did not deprive downstream proofs of the necessary information: the existing `_app` lemmas already characterized the natural transformation at the level where it was used. This is a reusable technique: marking a construction that already characterized by related lemmas `@[no_expose]`. However, it isn’t widely applicable, since there need to be suitable declaration with enough characterization to work on, for example even until now we didn’t find a way to replace the workaround by marking some `@[no_expose]`, because it is too close to the basic constructions of pullback and pushforward. Thus, `@[no_expose]` is particularly attractive when the existing API already describes the declaration sufficiently, but its implementation is likely to cause problems if exposed downstream. ### 1.2 Slow Derived Tensor A second issue arose while constructing the instance stating that the derived tensor product of *étale* sheaves is a left derivation of the ordinary tensor product. More precisely, we were constructing an `IsLeftDerivedFunctor₂` instance for `curriedTensor (DerivedCategory (Sheaf X.smallEtaleTopology A))`. Even providing a proof with exactly the expected type led to very slow kernel checking. We found that changing `Functor.IsLeftDerivedFunctor₂` from an `abbrev` to an `@[reducible] def` resolved the issue. This is because instead of `abbrev` that would expand in kernel directly, because any `def` is marked as regular, the kernel could use same-head argument comparison through lazy delta reduction i.e. doing `congr`, checking whether they are directly syntactically equal. (The `@[reducible]` attribute was only retained to preserve the intended elaboration behavior.) We are especially grateful to Professor Joël Riou for providing the first construction of the derived tensor product (in [Mathlib4 PR 25848](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/25848)). Based on this, here we managed to improve the performance of the surrounding development. As reflected in Mathlib4 `IsLeftDerivedFunctor₂`, the multivariate derived-functor definitions are now `@[reducible] def`s rather than `abbev`. ### 1.3 Timeout in the Derived-Completion Cone Another kernel timeout arose in an earlier development of derived completion, which has since been superseded. Although that implementation was not retained, diagnosing the timeout revealed a different source of expensive definitional equality. Simply declaring the derived-completion cone was enough to trigger the problem, even with its value replaced by `sorry`: ```lean noncomputable def DerivedCategory.derivedCompletionCone (K : DerivedCategory (Sheaf J (ModuleCat.{u + 1} R))) : Cone (DerivedCategory.quotPowFunctor J I ⋙ tensorLeft K) := sorry ``` *Code excerpt 4: A declaration that already caused a timeout.* In our investigation, `Kernel.check(type)` and `Kernel.check(value)` both completed in a reasonable time, whereas `Kernel.isDefEq(inferredType, declaredType)` timed out. The comparison involved proof terms that were not syntactically identical after Lean’s `abstractNestedProofs` processing. Such differences are ordinarily harmless because of proof irrelevance, but the kernel may still have to compare the propositions in which the proofs live. Here those propositions involved large proof-carrying instance expressions, including the `MonoidalCategory` instance on `DerivedCategory`, so the comparison could descend into a substantial amount of structure. One useful diagnostic experiment was to pass the derived-category `MonoidalCategory` instance as an explicit parameter, rather than having Lean infer the concrete instance; the corresponding check then completed quickly. The final solution is direct and preserved the intended construction: we gave the indexing diagram `DerivedCategory.quotPowFunctor J I ⋙ tensorLeft K` its own named definition and used that name in the type of the cone. Even an `abbrev` helped in this case. The named diagram provided a stable point of reference, so the kernel no longer had to compare independently expanded versions of the entire construction, including the proofs nested within it. ### 1.4 Slow Monoidal Pullback While working on the monoidality of pullback functors, we encountered two further, complementary patterns of expensive kernel conversion. Addressing both was necessary to resolve the performance problems in the file. First, comparing expressions beneath structure projections can be very expensive even when the underlying structures are cheaply definitionally equal. In our case, the kernel struggled with components of two natural transformations of the form `(τ.app X).app Y`, although the natural transformations themselves could be compared efficiently. We avoided asking the kernel to rediscover that equality after successive applications of `NatTrans.app`. Instead, we introduced a general congruence-style lemma that transports a componentwise equation along a propositional equality of natural transformations: ```lean lemma app_app_comp_of_eq (h : (τ.app X).app Y ≫ f = k) (σ : F ⟶ G) (hσ : σ = τ) : (σ.app X).app Y ≫ f = k := hσ ▸ h ``` The original proof ended with `exact h`, which required the kernel to establish a potentially expensive definitional equality beneath two applications of `NatTrans.app`. With the new lemma, the final `rfl` compares the natural transformations themselves, before taking their components. The essential optimization was therefore to move the equality obligation above the expensive projections, rather than merely splitting the proof into smaller lemmas. Second, passing a compatibility `Prop` to a generic constructor could trigger an expensive type conversion. Although the theorem’s type and the constructor’s expected binder proposition were definitionally equal, their elaborated expressions are not directly syntactically equal. Unfolding and comparing the large propositions could lead to extensive recursive reduction. We addressed this by giving the compatibility condition a stable name using an ordinary `def`. ```lean def LaxSquareHδ (δG : ...) (e : ...) : Prop := ∀ a b, (δG.app ...).app ... ≫ ... = ... noncomputable def ofLaxSquareHδ ... (hδ : LaxSquareHδ δG e) ... := Functor.OplaxMonoidal.ofLaxSquare ... hδ ... ``` We also supplied a bridge theorem whose declared type used precisely `LaxSquareHδ`. This served two related purposes. First, when the expected and supplied types shared the same regular-definition head, the kernel could try comparing their arguments before unfolding the potentially large proposition. Second, the bridge theorem isolated the remaining conversion in a separate kernel-checking context, where it proved substantially cheaper. An `abbrev` did not give the same benefit, because it led to more aggressive unfolding. These remedies addressed different bottlenecks. The first changed where a proof’s equality was established, while the second made the type of a proof argument easier for the kernel to match against the constructor’s expected binder type. Together they made the entire file as much as five times faster to check; applying either strategy alone still left a significant type-checking bottleneck. Taken together, these cases gave us a more systematic way to investigate kernel slowdowns and made it possible for coding agents to contribute to performance improvements. The broader lesson is that the mathematical content of a construction need not change in order to make it tractable for the kernel: a well-chosen abstraction or interface can prevent an otherwise expensive comparison. We still do not fully understand every slowdown, but these experiences have made such problems far more manageable. ## 2 Mathematical Design Choices in Formalization Beside pure technical issues, we learned that decisions related to mathematical design are crucial to formalizing correctly, choosing a workable setup, and making progress efficiently. These decisions are often implicit in conventional mathematical writing, but a formalization project must make them explicit at the right time. There are hidden or vague parts in natural language that needs to be pinned down, for example universe issue, which wouldn’t be exhibited in any natural language proof. Initially, we considered `X : Scheme.{u}` and a Grothendieck abelian coefficient category `A` of universe level `u`. In this setting, we could construct the sheafification of `A`-valued presheaves on the *étale* site of `X`. However, the corresponding construction for the *pro-étale* site could not use the same universe assignment. Unlike the *étale* site, the *pro-étale* site over `X` is not essentially small, and we did not have an analogous small dense subsite, such as `AffineEtale`, for case-specific hack. We therefore needed the target Grothendieck abelian category of universe level `u + 1`. Because this difference had not been anticipated, accommodating it required changes to signatures and constructions throughout a substantial part of the development. Identifying such constraints immediately after the blueprint stage, before large-scale formalization began, would have saved considerable rework. Apart from corners that haven’t being considered in natural language, the blueprint itself should also be adjusted for formalization, it cannot always use the same shorthand as a blueprint for human readers. For example, despite its suggestive notation, $Rf_!$ is not simply the total right-derived functor of the underived $f_!$. While I was not sufficiently familiar with this part of the mathematics thus not aware of this difference, Opus also didn’t notice and correct the implementation either. Similar ambiguities arise in the six-functor notation: identical symbols can refer to functors constructed with different coefficient categories, sometimes by quite different methods. A paper can often leave the coefficient category implicit, but doing so in a formalization blueprint can send an agent down the wrong path. Specifying the intended construction and disambiguating overloaded notation are therefore substantive parts of preparing a useful blueprint, not merely matters of presentation. The geometric assumptions should also be decided early. Restricting the six operations to bounded constructible derived categories requires carefully chosen geometric and coefficient hypotheses, involving conditions such as quasi-excellence and an $\ell$-coprime base scheme. For the part of the theory relevant to our project, choosing to work with schemes that are separated and of finite type over a field makes many of these hypotheses directly manageable. Without explicitly deciding on this particular separated, finite-type over field setup, an agent might select assumptions that are too strong, too weak, or incompatible with results needed later. Making that concrete choice early was therefore important. Other than the final setup we usually use, we also need to take care of the way how we construct them. For example, the six-functor formalism with $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ coefficients cannot simply be obtained by restricting the formalism for sheaves valued in `ModuleCat`, without considering the topology on the coefficient ring. Our initial plan was to construct the category of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$-sheaves as a 2-colimit of categories of sheaves with coefficients in finite extensions $E$, while retaining a forgetful functor that would realize the resulting objects as genuine $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$-sheaves. Besides the difficulty of formulating and implementing the required 2-colimit, this approach encountered a more structural problem: because the category of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$-sheaves has too many isomorphisms, it is not simply the union of the essential images of the inclusion functors, the morphisms between objects would therefore be more complicated. This motivated our move to a framework based on ring objects and module objects. Once we adopted the module-object perspective, we sought a more uniform way to handle coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_E$, $E$, and $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$. To construct the six functors uniformly, we needed a compatible Cartesian system of ring objects. A mathematical expert on the project pointed out the appropriate organizing idea: these ring objects should arise by pullback from a point, with the universal point corresponding to condensed rings. With this setup, we could place the unbounded six-functor constructions for all these coefficient systems in a common framework. Finally, there are some lessons on formalizing efficiently, especially for choosing the right level of generality. Early on, we wanted a uniform setting for the coefficient categories that might arise in étale sheaf theory, such as `ModuleCat` and `Ab`. Although mathematically natural, that generality imposed a significant upfront cost. In retrospect, a better sequence would have been to implement the concrete constructions for `ModuleCat` and `Ab` first, and then return to the question of how to treat them uniformly within a suitably general setup. Some abstractions turned out to be unhelpful altogether. We initially tried to organize the six-functor formalisms for the *étale* and *pro-étale* sites within a single framework. Their Lean implementations diverged at a very early stage, because the *pro-étale* setting uses quasi-compact covers, rather than relying only on joint surjectivity. While the general site-level pullback and pushforward constructions already occupied the natural common layer, there are no good abstractions to do, we therefore refactored the development into two frameworks directly specifying to the respective sites. This happened because at the early stage, we focused too much on creating big blocks for agents to work on, in this case they are *étale* proper base change and smooth base change. Even a modest amount of work on the *pro-étale* side at that stage would probably have exposed the mismatch much earlier. The lesson was not to avoid abstraction, but to test a proposed common framework against the distinct cases in the first place before investing heavily in it. --- lean4_performance_diagnostic_and_remediation_guide.md: this is a prompt for an agent to solve the kernel problem.
posts.title: Challenges and Lessons from Human-Led Formalization

posts.author: Bin Dong, Nailin Guan, Jiedong Jiang, Ruochuan Liu, Christian Merten, Xiangyu Pan, Tingxiao Shi, Bin Wu, Edison Xie and Wei Yang
posts.body: This is a repost of a blog post originally published on the Xena project, hosted by Kevin Buzzard, available at https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/11/a-modern-reorganization-of-mathematics/ > We mathematicians need to put far greater effort into communicating mathematical ideas. To accomplish this, we need to pay much more attention to communicating not just our definitions, theorems, and proofs, but also our ways of thinking. > > — William P. Thurston, *On Proof and Progress in Mathematics* (1994) Since the beginning of mathematical study, people have been trying to present mathematics and to communicate mathematical ideas. Mathematicians carefully choose names and symbols that match their intuitions in order to improve understanding. For most of this history, the medium for writing down a piece of mathematics has been linear text: a paper consisting of definitions, theorems, and proofs. In modern mathematics, however, the size and complexity of proofs and of the ideas behind them have grown rapidly. These now demand more and more effort both to write and to read. Various efforts have been made to reorganize and represent mathematics to enhance our understanding. The Bourbaki [[1](#ref-1)] group maintains a series of textbooks developing mathematics in a coherent way. The [Stacks Project](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu) [[7](#ref-7)] is an online textbook in algebraic geometry, in which theorems and definitions are tagged, linked and organized hierarchically by topic. [Kerodon](https://kerodon.net) [[3](#ref-3)] is a similar website for higher category theory. [Kedlaya’s web-based notes](https://kskedlaya.org/prismatic/) [[2](#ref-2)] offer another example in *p*-adic cohomology. Two further examples are worth noting. The [nLab](https://ncatlab.org) [[6](#ref-6)] is a collaborative wiki with an emphasis on ideas and abstract viewpoints. It is not organized hierarchically following the logical structure of proofs, but around concepts and their relations. [Mathlib](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4/) [[5](#ref-5)] on the other hand is a uniform formal library organized by mathematical field and containing every detail of proofs. ## Two Layers of Mathematics The last two expositions mentioned above represent two equally indispensable components of mathematics. On one side are the analogies, the slogans, the examples and even the hand-waving arguments that carry mathematical understanding. On the other side are the rigorous, detailed proofs that refine and realize vague ideas into sound arguments. We often think in the first style and write in the second. Consider an example from probability theory. If *X* and *Y* are independent random variables, then $$\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y).$$ A completely rigorous proof is easy to write down. Yet what guides us in proving and using this lemma is the picture of Pythagoras’ theorem. We argue that mathematical understanding needs both: High-level ideas and rigorous proofs. Slogans and analogies can convey why a proof strategy may work, but a strategy remains a strategy as long it has not been executed as a complete proof. A text consisting only of slogans walks on clouds. It may hold one up for a step or two, and then one falls. Conversely, a perfectly detailed proof alone does not provide a picture of the whole. This is precisely why reading a proof generated by AI can be so painful. Every step is correct, yet one has no sense of the underlying motivation. Explaining the high-level picture is similar to telling a story. However, adding storytelling into professional mathematical texts has been hard for several reasons. Choosing and computing a representative example takes effort. Worse, slogans and analogies are very easy to get wrong, and most people would rather not write at all if what they write is potentially wrong. And many proofs are conceptually clear, with the difficulty entirely technical. If one pushes through those technical difficulties to obtain a rigorous proof, that is what gets published. But nobody publishes the other text, saying “here is the argument I first had in mind, here is where it fails, and here is the repair.” This is also why people benefit much more from talking to mathematicians than from reading papers. The situation has improved recently. Large language models (LLMs) and agents are now extremely good at figuring out proofs and filling in tedious details. The technology of formalization guarantees the correctness of every detail by having a proof assistant check each step. LLMs are also improving rapidly at auto-formalization, to reduce manual formalization work. We are in a position to see AI reduce, rather than increase as at present, the burden of presenting mathematics, so that the two layers of mathematics can be brought together in one place, connected to each other. ## A Prototype The high-level ideas and the rigorous proof discussed above are the two ends of mathematical presentation. They can be connected by a series of successively refining layers. We want to present this refinement process directly to the reader, so that one can see the overall route of a proof and go all the way down into the details. For a large proof such as the Weil conjectures, one has a top-level picture consisting precisely of the analogies, dictionaries, and strategies described above. A Weil cohomology theory would immediately prove the conjectures, and ℓ-adic cohomology is one example. One then elaborates the argument, working out how each step is actually carried out to obtain a proof at a finer grain. The key properties of a Weil cohomology follow from the calculation of $f^!$ and the general formalism of the six operations on the (pro-)étale site. Step by step, the slogan-level argument is refined into something checkable down to the last detail. Through this process the vague story becomes a completely rigorous proof, and along the way one meets and resolves technical obstructions. As a concrete proposal, we have built [a prototype](https://weil-conjectures.merten.dev/) that attempts to organize and present a complete proof of the Weil conjectures in this way. It produces an artifact with two halves. The first is a multi-layered text presented as a website, a proof written at several levels of granularity and obtained by refining the top-level argument downwards, so that a reader can enter at whatever level of detail they want. The second is a formal artifact associated with the text, in which every step at the finest level is checked by a proof assistant, so that the whole proof is machine-verified. This layered structure also determines the division of labour between humans and AI. Humans discuss and decide the overall proof route ([see this detailed discussion](https://blueprint.fuxi.merten.dev/#/blog/proof-route-choices)), as well as the underlying key definitions and mathematical frameworks. As the argument is refined, LLMs begin to fill in the details of key theorems fixed by hand, while humans review and adjust. At the bottom, AI takes the human-readable but not yet fully rigorous text and expands every last detail on its own, then checks the result by formalization. Mathematical judgement thus sets the route, and AI makes it practical to carry the details all the way down to a machine-checked proof. We also invested human effort in formalizing the main framework of derived categories and the six operations on the (pro-)étale site, providing an early application in Riou’s work [[4](#ref-4)] on the formalization of derived categories and derived functors, and sharing human experience dealing with potential kernel performance issues ([see this detailed discussion](https://blueprint.fuxi.merten.dev/#/blog/lessons-from-formalization)). The formalization of detailed proofs is left entirely to auto-formalization. The bottom layer is one that a human could, but never has to, look at. People read the layer suited to them, which is compressed, comprehensible, and already detailed enough to show how the strategy actually works, knowing that the layer beneath it has been checked, so the proof is sound. We use a website to present the notes and the formalization together. It has a graph that displays both refinement relations and proof dependencies. A high-level node can be expanded into a box containing its refining nodes, and proof dependencies are drawn as arrows. Each node corresponds to a page, with high-level nodes carrying the story and low-level nodes carrying precise proofs linked to their formal counterparts. The website thus allows readers to enter at their desired level of detail and move between exposition and machine-checked proof. The webpages can also be reconstructed into conventional linear notes. All of this has become practical only through recent advances in LLMs and agents. Their mathematical proving ability helps elaborate the layered notes, auto-formalization capability helps complete the formal verification, and coding ability helps build the website presentation. In all three parts, humans only determine the high-level strategy and goals, while AI implements the details. This collaboration allows us to realize a modern reorganization of mathematics. ## An Entangled Web of Mathematics This is an early attempt to create a library combining both natural and formal language. Although the current prototype is built around a single huge proof of the Weil conjectures, we see it as extensible in the manner of the Stacks Project. Developing a new related body of theory, such as perverse sheaves or nearby and vanishing cycles, means that by the same process of refinement, the new proof decomposes into new parts and reusable parts already in the library. The same low-level details are organized into new high-level stories. In the dependency graph, this corresponds to adding or deleting some blocks while existing low-level blocks move around and regroup into new high-level blocks. Numerous mathematical ideas can be intertwined and linked with the shared details that support them. In this way, we weave an entangled web of mathematics. We hope that more, and in time perhaps most, of mathematics can be reorganized in a multi-layered way. To make this practical, we need to summarize and share transferable experiences from such projects, so that human effort becomes more efficient and can be concentrated on the highest-level mathematical decisions. Imagine a comprehensive library of natural-language mathematics in which countless top-level core ideas are written down, displayed, expanded, and grounded in detail, and in which the bottom is guaranteed correct by formalization. If we could work on mathematics in this way, thinking and writing at the top level, collaborating with AI to fill in the middle, and letting AI handle the bottom entirely automatically, it might be a fascinating new way to study and understand or even extend the entangled web of mathematics. ## References - [1] Nicolas Bourbaki. *Éléments de mathématique*. Paris: Hermann, 1939–. - [2] Kiran S. Kedlaya. [*Notes on Prismatic Cohomology*](https://kskedlaya.org/prismatic/) (visited 5 November 2026). - [3] Jacob Lurie. [*Kerodon*](https://kerodon.net) (visited 5 November 2026). - [4] Joël Riou. “Formalization of derived categories in Lean/mathlib”. *Annals of Formalized Mathematics* 1 (July 2025), pp. 1–42. [doi: 10.46298/afm.13609](https://doi.org/10.46298/afm.13609). - [5] The mathlib Community. [*mathlib*](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4/) (visited 5 November 2026). - [6] The nLab Authors. [*The nLab*](https://ncatlab.org) (visited 5 November 2026). - [7] The Stacks Project Authors. [*The Stacks Project*](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu) (visited 5 November 2026).

posts.body: The notes on the Weil conjectures were prepared through a collaboration between a human and AI. Without AI assistance, it would have been impossible to produce 370 pages of notes in a reasonable amount of time. We used GPT-6.1-sol to fill in mathematical details and carefully prompted Claude Opus 5.5 to improve the writing. All proof routes were determined by the human at the beginning. ## 1. Building the Proof Skeleton Once we’ve settled on the proof route, we organize the notes around a skeleton made up of the final theorem and its key intermediate theorems. This structure serves two purposes: it shows readers the main thread of the argument, and it gives the later formalization a clear set of verification targets. With the development of LLMs, they have acquired tremendous advantages, at least in assisting with the study and retrieval of existing mathematical knowledge. This provides the conditions necessary for the following workflow. To grasp the overall structure of a proof, we first ask an LLM to generate what might be called a rough set of lecture notes or a proof outline. This outline may be rough, but it should clarify the main components of the proof. In practice, we once attempted to refine such an outline further: starting from the key nodes in the rough notes, we asked the model to expand them recursively until every leaf node corresponded to something already available in Mathlib, thereby producing a proof that included virtually every detail. This amounted to writing a natural-language text from the perspective of formalization. The approach arose from our lack of confidence in the ability of LLMs to write Lean code: we once believed that every detail needed to be specified in advance. In reality, however, this process proved extremely slow. It could easily become trapped in an almost endless expansion of details, with no clear criterion for when to stop, much as a formalization project can continually generate new `sorry`s without any predictable endpoint. Once a reasonable proof has been expanded to roughly ten times its original length, its details become unmanageable for a human reader. Therefore, this approach is largely unusable as a workflow. Nevertheless, this strategy of “growing downward to Mathlib” is not entirely infeasible. The key is to skip over sufficiently large blocks of detail: that is, to select standard material that one has good reason to believe can be formalized without much difficulty and for which detailed treatments already exist, such as certain chapters of the Stacks Project. This is sufficient to generate, for each key theorem, a plausible proof roadmap that appears to avoid circular dependencies. By fixing the main proof strategy while providing only abbreviated proofs for those parts that might otherwise require substantial external material, we obtain the skeleton of the lecture notes. ## 2. Writing for Mathematical Understanding Once the skeleton is in place, the next step is to turn the proof route into text that actually conveys mathematical understanding. At this point, the LLM’s writing ability becomes critical—and this ability can’t be divorced from its understanding of the mathematics. After all, a skilled novelist or poet won’t necessarily write mathematics well, since they may not understand the mathematical content involved (though there are rare exceptions). For this reason, before beginning the actual writing, or at least at a relatively early stage, we should have the LLM develop its own understanding of both the overall proof structure and the details of the individual arguments. Only then can the writing change the form without altering the substance. It was precisely for this reason that we switched from GPT to Claude Opus 5.5 for the main writing process. Even without elaborate instructions, and with only basic guidance on matters such as notation and the organization of material, an LLM can produce a reasonably satisfactory text. At this stage, we can have the LLM study a large number of well-written papers and other materials to learn the writing style of particular mathematicians, thereby capturing certain rules or expectations that are difficult to articulate precisely. We can also specify an intended audience to help an LLM decide which parts deserve more detailed treatment and which can be presented more briefly. Since human attention and energy are limited, we can additionally ask the LLM to simulate readers with the appropriate mathematical background and evaluate the text from their perspective, identifying areas in need of improvement. For those aspects of the workflow that have not yet been optimized, we believe that principles accompanied by both positive and negative examples are more effective in guiding an LLM’s writing than abstract principles alone. When necessary, human authors should revise portions of the text themselves to provide concrete examples that help the LLM understand what is actually required. Furthermore, the distinctive ideas that human authors wish to convey should be deliberately incorporated into this workflow. This is important not only for calibrating the LLM’s writing, but also for preserving diversity in mathematical exposition. Indeed, there are often multiple viable paths from one statement to the next. The author’s choice of a particular path, together with the decision of where to elaborate and where to omit details, is itself an expression of mathematical judgment and values. What the writing should convey is precisely these choices and the reasons behind them, rather than merely a neutral route through the proof.
posts.title: How We Prepared Notes on the Weil Conjectures

posts.author: Xiangyu Pan
posts.body: *Abstract.* We explain the rationale behind the choice of constructions and proofs in our blueprint for the Weil conjectures. Our approach favors ordinary categories, the reuse of existing foundations, and a small collection of widely applicable tools. This note records the rationale behind our proof-route choices in the Weil conjectures. We first state the general principles that guide the proof as a whole ([§1](#sec-1)), then discuss the choices made for individual topics ([§2](#sec-2)). The route itself uses modern methods for a good part of the argument, some of which have not been written down in this setting before. ## 1. Guiding principles **Ordinary categories.** We work only with 1-categories. Using higher category theory, such as 2-categories or $\infty$-categories, would make the proof depend on an unnecessarily large input; formalizing it would also considerably enlarge the project without being necessary for the results we use. **Avoiding local acyclicity and vanishing cycles.** We avoid the general formalism of local acyclicity and of nearby and vanishing cycles [[SGA7II](#ref-SGA7II), Exp. XIII]. Besides its technical geometric inputs, this formalism introduces delicate functoriality and equivariance issues. In the derived 1-category, taking a cone is not in general functorial, so defining vanishing cycles as a cone does not by itself provide their functoriality; higher-categorical enhancements express this functoriality and its coherences more naturally. Avoiding this formalism therefore keeps the proof within our chosen foundations and reduces the work needed to manage Galois actions and specialization. **Weil II and $\ell$-adic coefficients.** We choose the route via weight theory in *Weil II* [[D2](#ref-D2)] over the route via Lefschetz pencils in *Weil I* [[D1](#ref-D1)]: the result of *Weil II* is more general than that of *Weil I*; weight theory and the Fourier transform tend to be used more broadly in the literature than Lefschetz-pencil theory; and the improved Fourier-transform proof adopted here avoids vanishing cycles ([§2.6](#sec-2-6)), whereas the Lefschetz-pencil proof relies on them. For coefficients we choose $\ell$-adic, specifically pro-étale, cohomology. Pro-étale cohomology is already available in Mathlib, and the `proetale` repository [[JM](#ref-JM)] formalizes the comparison theorems with étale cohomology, so this material can be reused rather than developed from scratch. By contrast, the $p$-adic alternative relevant here is rigid cohomology, which would require developing a separate foundation, including rigid analytic spaces. ## 2. Choices for individual topics The choices below are grouped by topic; each records what we chose and why. ### 2.1. Constructible derived categories **Pro-étale rather than classical adic systems.** The pro-étale topology of Bhatt–Scholze [[BS](#ref-BS), §§3–6] gives a cleaner treatment of adic coefficients. Classically, coefficients are encoded by systems of étale sheaves; in the pro-étale setting, one has repleteness and actual coefficient sheaves $\mathcal{O}_{E,X}$ and $E_X$ for an arbitrary algebraic extension $E/\mathbb{Q}_\ell$. This makes the constructible categories more natural to formulate. In the noetherian setting it also simplifies the definitions and provides a uniform foundation for the six functors needed later [[BS](#ref-BS), §6.8]. **The condensed approach.** We also use the perspective of Hemo–Richarz–Scholbach [[HRS](#ref-HRS), Def. 3.3, §7], which treats lisse and constructible objects with finite, $\mathcal{O}_E$- or $E$-coefficients uniformly on arbitrary schemes. Although their paper is written using $\infty$-categories, we need only selected results that can be stated and proved using ordinary categories and derived 1-categories. We adopt these results for their uniformity and generality without taking on the full higher-categorical framework of the paper. ### 2.2. Proper and smooth base change We use the Stacks Project proofs of proper and smooth base change [Stacks, Tags [`095T`](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095T), [`0EYU`](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYU)]. The proper-base-change argument remains close to SGA 4, while the direct smooth-base-change argument avoids the local-acyclicity formalism used in the classical organization [[SGA4](#ref-SGA4), Exp. XVI]. Their use of curve cohomology fits well with the Jacobian theory that is also needed later in this project. ### 2.3. Smooth purity For purity of smooth pairs, we choose the method of deformation to the normal cone. It uses normal bundles, vector bundles, and $\mathbb{A}^1$-invariance, which are useful beyond this particular theorem. This is more rewarding for the reader, since the same construction is used in intersection theory [[Ful](#ref-Ful), Chap. 5] and homotopy purity [[MV](#ref-MV), §3.2]. ### 2.4. The trace formula **Lefschetz–Verdier rather than curve correspondences.** We use the Lefschetz–Verdier pairing of SGA 5 [[SGA5](#ref-SGA5), Exp. III]. The Nielsen–Wecken type route in SGA 4½ [[SGA4½](#ref-SGA4half), *Rapport sur la formule des traces*], also followed by the Stacks Project [Stacks, Tags [`03U1`](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03U1), [`03UF`](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03UF)], uses Weil’s fixed-point theorem for curves [[Wei](#ref-Wei)]. Taking that route would require developing Weil’s classical algebraic geometry and classical, non-derived intersection theory. The Lefschetz–Verdier pairing instead reuses our six-functor formalism and is useful for later applications. **The Künneth formula.** For the ordinary, non-compact-support Künneth formula needed in the Künneth–Verdier isomorphism, we choose the direct Stacks Project proof [Stacks, Tag [`0F1P`](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F1P)] to avoid the general acyclicity machinery. For the pairing itself we follow SGA 5 rather than the relative formulation of Lu–Zheng [[LZ](#ref-LZ)]: the latter’s 2-categorical framework and broader relative setting would add more work beyond our application over a finite field. ### 2.5. Weil sheaves **Rank-one geometric monodromy.** For smooth geometrically connected curves, we use the proof based on the $\ell$-adic logarithm and Jacobians, which are already available for computing the cohomology of curves in the proof of the base change theorems. This replaces the proof in [[D2](#ref-D2), §1.3], which uses class field theory, and thereby avoids developing it. **Monodromy and determinant weights.** We use variants of the arguments in [[D2](#ref-D2), §1.3] that isolate the facts about reductive groups needed for the determinant weight results. These require some basic results on reductive groups, instead of the classification of reductive groups. **The twist lemma.** We use an elementary proof of the twist reduction for irreducible lisse Weil sheaves, rather than deriving it from the geometric monodromy results as in [[D2](#ref-D2), Prop. 1.3.14]. This reduces its prerequisites of the trace formula for Weil sheaves. ### 2.6. The Deligne–Laumon estimate We use a further refinement of the Fourier–Deligne approach, taking Kiehl–Weissauer’s treatment [[KW](#ref-KW), Chap. I] as a reference. This version is not Laumon’s original argument [[Lau](#ref-Lau)], but a refinement that avoids vanishing cycles. Compared with Deligne’s original proof [[D2](#ref-D2), §3] and Laumon’s original development, it has the advantage of a smaller set of prerequisites compatible with our 1-categorical foundations. We restrict perverse sheaf theory to the perverse $t$-structure and middle extension on curves. This is enough for the chosen estimate and avoids the cost of developing the general theory in all dimensions. The resulting weight theorem retains the generality that motivated our choice of the Weil II route. ## References - [BS] B. Bhatt and P. IHÉS **43** (1974), 273–307. [doi:10.1007/BF02684373](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02684373). - [D2] P. Deligne, *La conjecture de Weil. II*, Publ. Math. IHÉS **52** (1980), 137–252. [doi:10.1007/BF02684780](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02684780). - [Ful] W. Merten, *Proétale cohomology in Lean*, GitHub repository, [`https://github.com/chrisflav/proetale`](https://github.com/chrisflav/proetale), accessed 30 October 2026. - [KW] R. Kiehl and R.
